extracted.intended_audience: students and teachers of mathematics; authors of mathematics textbooks; problem-solvers learning heuristics
extracted.subtask_description: Heuristic and pedagogical guidance for solving, checking, presenting, and deriving mathematical problems: introduction and choice of auxiliary problems, methods to find reductions, tests and checks, order of exposition, and the interplay of intuition and formal proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Introduce auxiliary elements with clear motivation
rubrics_metrics.description: Teachers and authors of textbooks should not forget that the intelligent student and the intelligent reader are not satisfied by verifying that the steps of a reasoning are correct but also want to know the motive and the purpose of the various steps. The introduction of an auxiliary element is a conspicuous step. If a tricky auxiliary line appears abruptly in the figure, without any motivation, and solves the problem surprisingly, intelligent students and readers are disappointed; they feel that they are cheated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make auxiliary steps comprehensible by suitable remarks or by carefully chosen questions and suggestions (see referenced sections). Although it takes time and effort, explaining the motive and purpose of conspicuous steps is worthwhile pedagogically.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of an auxiliary problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Auxiliary problem is a problem which we consider, not for its own sake, but because we hope that its consideration may help us to solve another problem, our original problem. The original problem is the end we wish to attain, the auxiliary problem a means by which we try to attain our end.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat the auxiliary problem as a tool or intermediate task: its unknown may be an auxiliary unknown introduced to simplify or reframe the original problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Possible profits from an auxiliary problem
rubrics_metrics.description: The profit that we derive from the consideration of an auxiliary problem may be of various kinds. We may use the result of the auxiliary problem; or we may use the method of the auxiliary problem; or it may be instructive or have aesthetic appeal; or it may open unexplored possibilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: (1) use auxiliary unknown substitution to reduce degree (algebraic example), (2) use analogous simpler plane problem to learn methods for a solid geometry problem. Examine whether you can use result, method, or instruction from the auxiliary problem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Risk and judgment in choosing auxiliary problems
rubrics_metrics.description: We take away from the original problem the time and the effort that we devote to the auxiliary problem. If our investigation of the auxiliary problem fails, the time and effort we devoted to it may be lost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Exercise judgment: choose auxiliary problems that appear more accessible, instructive, aesthetically appealing, or offering unexplored possibilities. Avoid choosing auxiliaries solely because you are tired of the original problem. Weigh potential profit against the time/effort risk.

rubrics_metrics.name: How to find auxiliary problems (heuristics)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is no infallible method of discovering suitable auxiliary problems. There are, however, questions and suggestions which are frequently helpful, as LOOK AT THE UNKNOWN. We are often led to useful auxiliary problems by VARIATION OF THE PROBLEM.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use heuristics such as examining the unknown, varying parameters, analogy, generalization/specialization, decomposing and recombining parts, and asking targeted questions to suggest natural auxiliary constructions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equivalent problems / convertible (bilateral) reduction
rubrics_metrics.description: Two problems are equivalent if the solution of each involves the solution of the other. The passage from the original problem to the auxiliary problem is called convertible reduction, or bilateral reduction, or equivalent reduction if these two problems, the original and the auxiliary, are equivalent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Convertible reductions are often more desirable because equivalent problems share the same solutions; use them when possible to avoid losing or admitting extraneous solutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Check equivalence when reducing (avoid narrowing/widening)
rubrics_metrics.description: If we pass from a proposed condition to a new condition equivalent to it, we have the same solutions. But if we pass from a proposed condition to a narrower one, we lose solutions, and if we pass to a wider one we admit improper, adventitious solutions which have nothing to do with the proposed problem.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Carefully check the nature of each newly introduced condition: Is it equivalent to the original condition? This is especially important for systems of equations or geometric construction problems.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chains of equivalent auxiliary problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Chains of equivalent auxiliary problems are frequent in mathematical reasoning: reduce A to B to C ... until a last problem L whose solution is known or immediate. Each problem being equivalent to the preceding, the last problem L must be equivalent to our original problem A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use successive equivalent reductions to reach a known problem; this classical method was used by Greek mathematicians (Pappus) and is valid if equivalence is preserved at each step.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unilateral reduction (to more or less ambitious problems) and its risks
rubrics_metrics.description: If, from a proposed problem, we pass either to a more ambitious or to a less ambitious auxiliary problem we call the step a unilateral reduction. There are two kinds of unilateral reduction, and both are, in some way or other, more risky than a bilateral or convertible reduction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Unilateral reductions can work (e.g., specialization sometimes helps; generalization can lead to the Inventor's Paradox), but they are riskier: solving the auxiliary may not give the full solution of the original. Use supplementary remarks or extra steps to recover the original solution when possible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Testing numerical results by comparison and commonsense estimates
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical results of mathematical problems can be tested by comparing them to observed numbers, or to a commonsense estimate of observable numbers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Especially for problems arising from practical needs, compare computed numbers with observation or reasonable estimates to catch glaring errors or careless use of data.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tests: specialization, dimensional analysis, and variation of data
rubrics_metrics.description: We may test formulas by SPECIALIZATION (set parameters to special values), TEST BY DIMENSION (check physical dimension consistency), and by VARIATION OF THE DATA (see whether increasing inputs increases/decreases outputs as expected).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply these tests not only to final results but also to intermediate results. Preparing to use such tests may involve generalizing numeric problems to problems in letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Checking the argument — avoid mere repetition; vary the check
rubrics_metrics.description: Checking the argument step-by-step, we should avoid mere repetition. Mere repetition is apt to become boring and is likely to repeat the same stumble. If it is necessary to go again through the whole argument step by step, we should at least change the order of the steps, or their grouping, to introduce some variation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is often more interesting and effective to pick the weakest point and examine it first. Use the question DID YOU USE ALL THE DATA? to locate weak points.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seek alternative derivations and reinterpret parts of results
rubrics_metrics.description: Can you derive the result differently? When the solution obtained is long and involved, we suspect there is some clearer and less roundabout solution. Two proofs are better than one.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Study the result to find intuitive interpretations of parts (as with the frustum example) and pursue these small reinterpretations; they may accumulate to a simpler proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exploit results by deriving new problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Having found a result, inquire whether there is something more behind it and whether you can use the result or the method for some other problem. We can easily imagine new problems if we are somewhat familiar with the principal means of varying a problem (GENERALIZATION, SPECIALIZATION, ANALOGY, DECOMPOSING AND RECOMBINING).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Derive new problems by interchanging unknowns and data, by generalizing or specializing, by analogy, or by varying certain elements. Good problems often grow in clusters—look around when successful.

rubrics_metrics.name: Devising (heuristic) vs carrying out (rigorous) the solution plan
rubrics_metrics.description: We may use provisional and merely plausible arguments when devising the final and rigorous argument (like scaffolding). When the solution is sufficiently advanced we brush aside provisional arguments and accept only conclusive, strict arguments when carrying out the plan.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be generous with heuristic reasoning during invention but switch to painstaking checking in carrying out: check each step and ensure correctness. The more carefully you check steps in carrying out, the more freely you may use heuristics when devising.

rubrics_metrics.name: Order of working out details and choice of exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: We should give consideration to the order in which we work out the details, especially for complex problems. It is not reasonable to check minor details before we have good reasons to believe the major steps are sound. The order of writing down details may differ from the order of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Euclid's exposition (data → unknown; hypothesis → conclusion) is excellent for checking detail but often poor for showing the main line of argument. For teaching or conveying ideas, present an intuitive sketch of the main idea first and give Euclidean details afterwards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intuition and formal proof are complementary; verify by both
rubrics_metrics.description: The conscientious mathematician tries to see a proposition intuitively and to give a formal proof. Intuitive insight and formal proof are two different ways of perceiving the truth; intuition may rush ahead of formal proof and vice versa.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When checking steps, rely on intuition or formal rules as appropriate, and try to do both when possible. Attempting to prove formally what is seen intuitively and to see intuitively what is proved formally is an invigorating exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Teach and cultivate the skill of devising auxiliary problems
rubrics_metrics.description: To devise an auxiliary problem is an important operation of the mind. To raise a clear-cut new problem subservient to another problem, to conceive distinctly as an end what is means to another end, is a refined achievement of the intelligence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Make devising auxiliaries an explicit teaching goal: provide questions, demonstrations of methods (LOOK AT THE UNKNOWN, VARIATION OF THE PROBLEM), and guided practice so students learn to handle auxiliary problems intelligently.
